KERNAL status and scratch ($90-$B1). STATUS ($90) is $40, the end of file of the last LOAD; no file is open ($98 = 0); the default devices are the keyboard and the screen ($99/$9A = 0 and 3). KERNAL screen-editor, keyboard and RS-232 workspace ($C7-$FC). The values are left from the stock 40 by 25 screen at $0400 before the game took over; the game's own screen is at $CC00, and the engine touches them only wholesale: the opening copies the zero page to $A002-$A0FF ($06B2), and SWAP_ZERO_PAGE_AND_BACKUP ($053E) exchanges $02-$FF with that copy around each part's load ($04FB, $0521), so the KERNAL has these values back while it loads. SCNKEY and GETIN, which the game calls, use some of them.

KERNAL LDTB1 ($D9-$F2) - the screen editor's 26-byte line-link table: one entry per screen row plus an editor scratch byte. Each entry is the high byte of its row's first screen address, with bit 7 set when the row is the first physical line of a logical line; the editor uses only bits 0-1 of it, ORed with HIBASE ($0288). The $84/$85/$86/$87 pattern here describes a stock 40x25 screen based at $0400, i.e. state left over from before the game took the machine. The game neither reads nor writes it.
Zero at the opening, and nothing in the engine uses it. The tape loader remnant at $9722-$9875, which never runs, stores its bytes through ($FD).

$0100-$01D7: code left in the stack page by the depacker that unpacked this copy of the game. It copies memory with $01 = $34, unpacks it with a run-length scheme whose escape byte is $D3 ($01C1), and ends by setting $01 = $37 and jumping to $3300. The game never runs it; its stack only uses the top of the page.
$01D8-$01EE: bytes left by earlier use of the stack.

The stack in use at the opening ($01EF-$01FF, stack pointer $EE). BASIC's input buffer ($0200-$0258); the game never uses it. It still holds the tokenised RUN ($8A) and the end of LOAD"THE NEVER. STORY",8,1, the commands that started the game.

KERNAL_LAT ($0259-$0262) - KERNAL table of active logical file numbers, one byte per open
file, up to ten. All zero: no logical file is open. Maintained by OPEN/CLOSE,
not by this program.
KERNAL_FAT ($0263-$026C) - KERNAL table of device numbers, parallel to KERNAL_LAT.
KERNAL_SAT ($026D-$0276) - KERNAL table of secondary addresses, parallel to KERNAL_LAT.

KEYBOARD_BUFFER (KEYD, $0277-$0280) - the KERNAL's ten-byte keystroke FIFO.
SCNKEY ($FF9F) scans the keyboard matrix through CIA 1 and appends PETSCII codes here,
bumping the count in NDX ($00C6); GETIN ($FFE4) removes the oldest code and decrements NDX.
The fill limit is XMAX ($0289), default 10.
This program never touches the buffer directly, but it is squarely on the input path: $0552
and $084B call SCNKEY, $0555 and $084E call GETIN, and $083A zeroes NDX to flush pending
keystrokes before reading a command line. Empty at the opening.

KERNAL HIBASE: high byte of the current screen-memory base. $04 selects the standard screen at $0400.
KERNAL XMAX: maximum number of characters accepted in the keyboard buffer. The default $0A permits ten queued characters.
KERNAL RPTFLG: keyboard auto-repeat mode. Zero, the power-up value, makes only the cursor keys, INST/DEL and the space bar repeat.

KERNAL KOUNT: the key-repeat countdown that SCNKEY counts down while a key is held, repeating the key when it runs out. The game zeroes it after each key the line editor accepts ($087D) and when play starts ($0763).

CALL_INIT_GAME ($0406)
Purpose: Non-returning entry into game initialisation, reached by falling through from ENTRY_POINT after the opening ($0403) and by the restart path (JMP from RESTART_GAME at $0FEE). Calls INIT_GAME to rebuild adventure state and the starting room, then falls through into MAIN_LOOP.
Inputs: None in registers.
Outputs: Adventure state rebuilt and the starting room described; control continues in MAIN_LOOP. Never returns to its caller.
Assumptions: The gameplay memory layout, banking, raster IRQ and display are already established; only the adventure state is rebuilt, after SHOW_PART_LOAD_SCREEN has loaded a part whenever LOADED_PART_NO ($5E) is not 0 (INIT_GAME_RUN $14E9).
Clobbers: A, X, Y, flags, and all game state through callees. The stack is not unwound here: RESTART_GAME pulls three return addresses, which reaches the main loop's level for a restart from a turn or room script, but after QUIT, a rule's action four calls deep, the return from PARSE_INPUT into MAIN_LOOP stays on the stack.
Hardware changes: None directly. Callees write screen and colour RAM through the terminal, and when a part is loaded SHOW_PART_LOAD_SCREEN blanks and re-enables the display, rewrites $D01A, stops CIA 1 timer A and drives the serial bus.

MAIN_LOOP ($0409)
Purpose: The non-returning foreground command loop: run the turn scripts (the resident one, the part's and the current room's, $147D), read one edited command line, parse and execute it, repeat forever.
Inputs: None in registers. Requires a part's data at $2F00 and initialised game state.
Outputs: Continuously updated screen and game-state arrays. Never returns; the only exits are the non-local ones taken by RESTART_GAME and ACTION_NEXT_PART.
Assumptions: Runs under the already-established gameplay banking ($01=$06), the raster-split IRQ, and the split display; it does not configure them itself.
Clobbers: A, X, Y, flags, and the whole parser, VM and renderer workspace.
Hardware changes: None directly; callees write screen RAM at $CC00-$CFFF, colour RAM at $D800-$DBFF and the bitmap at $E000, and read the CIA 1 keyboard matrix through KERNAL SCNKEY/GETIN.

SWITCH_TO_NEXT_PART ($0415)
Purpose: Move on to the next part of the story. Increments CURRENT_PART_NO, sets CURRENT_ROOM to that part's starting room ($34 for part 2, $4D for any later part), shows the swap prompt and loads, runs the new part's initialisation, and resumes the command loop.
Inputs: CURRENT_PART_NO ($2940) valid; the replacement disk part available in the drive.
Outputs: CURRENT_PART_NO incremented, CURRENT_ROOM set, $2F00-$95FF replaced by the next part's file, LOADED_PART_NO ($5E) recorded, and control transferred to MAIN_LOOP. Non-returning with respect to the action handler that invoked it.
Assumptions: Called only from ACTION_NEXT_PART, which has already discarded three levels of return address, so the stack is at the main-loop level.
Clobbers: A, X, Y, flags, UI and disk scratch, and whatever the new part's start script writes.
Hardware changes: Through its callees: VIC-II display enable, VIC interrupt enable $D01A, CIA 1 timer A control $DC0E, and the serial bus through the KERNAL's LOAD.

SHOW_PART_LOAD_SCREEN ($0439)
Purpose: Print sentence $2F, "Hit space to load", and the part's name on the same line (sentence $30 + CURRENT_PART_NO: "Part one!", "Part two!" or "Part three!", printed in lower case), wait for Space, then load the next part through the loader at $9700 and record which part is in memory.
Inputs: CURRENT_PART_NO ($2940), added to $30, picks the sentence that names the part. It does not choose the file: the loader adds one to the digit in its own file name before each load, so it loads PART 1, PART 2 and PART 3 in turn.
Outputs: The two sentences printed; the next PART file loaded over $2F00-$95FF; LOADED_PART_NO ($5E) set to CURRENT_PART_NO; returns normally.
Assumptions: Terminal, keyboard, the installed loader at $9700 and the drive are all available. Gameplay interrupts are suspended and restored by PREPARE_DISK_IO/END_DISK_IO around the load.

Purpose: Complete but unreachable KERNAL restore-game implementation: prompt for a filename, LOAD the saved state block over OBJECT_LOCATIONS, pull in a different story part if the restored save belongs to one, then redescribe and repaint the room.

Outputs: On success the saved state block is in memory, the room is redescribed and the picture repainted. On a carry-set KERNAL error it tail-jumps to DISK_IO_ERROR. Returns normally otherwise.
Assumptions: Static audit finds no call, pointer, action script or decoded operand reaching $0461 in the shipped build, so this routine is retained but inactive; the SAVE/LOAD verbs dispatch to the no-op stubs instead. DISK_IO_ERROR ($04B6)
Purpose: Shared failure tail for the retained disk subsystem: restore the gameplay machine state, raise the error flag, and print the disk-error message.
Inputs: Entered by tail jump from DISK_LOAD_GAME ($0478) or DISK_SAVE_GAME ($04B0) with carry set from the KERNAL call, or from ABORT_EMPTY_FILENAME at the $04B9 continuation.

ABORT_EMPTY_FILENAME ($04C3)
Purpose: Abort the filename prompt when the player entered nothing. Discards the immediate caller's return address so control cannot fall back into the load flow, then joins the error tail at $04B9.
Inputs: Entered by branch from READ_FILENAME ($04D5) with INPUT_LEN ($26) zero.
Outputs: Two bytes popped from the stack; DISK_ERROR_FLAG set to 1 and sentence $12 printed; the eventual RTS returns to the caller of the routine that called READ_FILENAME.
Assumptions: The stack contains exactly READ_FILENAME's return address on top, i.e. this label is only reachable from inside READ_FILENAME.
Clobbers: A, X, Y, flags, DISK_ERROR_FLAG, the two stack bytes of READ_FILENAME's return address, and renderer scratch.
Hardware changes: Writes screen and colour RAM through the terminal; no device register is programmed here.

READ_FILENAME ($04C8)

($0DE3). $FE separates rules, $FF ends the script.

It ends with action $07 (RETURN_SKIP_CALLER), which pops the interpreter's self-modified JSR
frame and returns straight to RUN_TURN_SCRIPTS, so the trailing $FF is unreachable.

TOKEN_POINTERS_TABLE — 94 little-endian pointers, one per compressed-text dictionary token.
A prose byte with bit 7 set is a token reference: the renderer clears bit 7, doubles the
remaining 0..93 id and reads the word at TOKEN_POINTERS_TABLE + 2*id. The pointer addresses a
dictionary record, so ids $80-$DD are defined and $DE-$FF have no entry.
The 94 pointers occupy $25DD-$2698; the records they address begin immediately afterwards at
$2699 (WORD_THE_LC) and run to $28B8.

Compressed-text dictionary records, $2699-$28B8. Each record is one length byte followed by
exactly that many ASCII characters, with no terminator and no padding; records are packed back
to back and are reached only through TOKEN_POINTERS_TABLE ($25DD), never by scanning.
The dictionary stores case-sensitive duplicates because prose is emitted verbatim: "the"
($2699) and "The" ($27CF), "to" ($26DB) and "To" ($2805), "There" ($26AB) and "there" ($2730),
"You" ($26D3) and "you" ($28B5) are separate tokens. Labels ending _LC or _CAP mark the

Never read or written by the game, and the same in every copy compared. Runs of $FF and $00 with odd bits set, like a C64's RAM at power-on: inferred to be what that memory held on the machine that saved the game.

Volume fade, the first thing MUSIC_PLAY does each frame: add the fade speed $F084 to the accumulator $F083. With a positive speed, a carry turns the volume $F082 up one step ($96C7); with a negative speed, no carry turns it down one ($96BF); speed 0 leaves it. Speed $0A raises the volume a step every 25.6 frames, $FB lowers it a step every 51.2.

The tune's once-a-frame entry, called from the opening's interrupt at $A884 with $01 = $05, which shows the RAM under the KERNAL where the tune's data lies: the fade, then voice 1 ($979D), voice 2 ($9A8C) and voice 3 ($9CF2), whose RTS returns to the interrupt.

Stops the tune: $19 = $38 (no voice reads the tune, all marked cut), fade speed and accumulator 0, the three voices' release counters ($F01D, $F048, $F073) 0 so no effect runs, and 0 in SID registers $D400-$D417; the volume in $D418 stays. Called at $0703 before the tune starts and at $15CC when a key ends the opening. Every command a voice's handler table does not use points here, so such a command would stop the music.
The volume one step down, unless it is already 0.
The volume one step up, unless it is already 15.
X, cut to four bits, becomes the volume $F082 and goes to $D418, which also clears the filter-mode bits.

Starts the tune from the top, called at $0706. For voices 3, 2 and 1 (X = 2, 1, 0): $19 = $3F, the voice's ticks ($1A,X) = 1 so it reads its first event next frame, its stack index ($1D,X) = $0F, and in its 84-byte block (offset $F08B,X from $9EF3) transpose 0, vibrato flags 0, pulse flags 0 and $0F in byte $22. The six bytes $F085-$F08A go to $10-$15: the voices start at $F250, $F5F3 and $F6BE. The volume is not set: voice 1's fifth command, after its lengths, envelope and two pokes, runs $F400 (the $9C at $F25C), which fades it in from whatever $F082 holds.

From here to $98FF the disk loader takes the driver's place when the opening ends ($0730 copies it from $C000), and $0453 calls $9700 to load each part. In the opening it is the middle of MUSIC_INIT: the second half of the start words from $F088,X into $13,X (voice 2's high byte, then voice 3's low and high bytes), then the next voice.
MUSIC_INIT's RTS. Once the loader is in place this byte is the digit of "PART n", which its INC $9708 (at $C009 before the move) advances before each load.
Voice 1's pulse sweep starts again from the base width: X/Y = $F018/$F019, then on into the start below.
Starts voice 1's pulse sweep at the width in X/Y: current width $F021/$F022 = X/Y, then the counters reload below.
Reloads voice 1's pulse counters: phase A steps $F028 = $F013, phase B steps $F029 = $F014, step timer $F02A = $F016.
Voice 3's pulse sweep starts again from the base width: X/Y = $F06E/$F06F, then on into the start below.
Starts voice 3's pulse sweep at the width in X/Y: current width $F077/$F078 = X/Y, then the counters reload below.
Reloads voice 3's pulse counters: step timer $F080 = $F06C, phase A steps $F07E = $F069, phase B steps $F07F = $F06A.
Voice 1's vibrato starts again from the note's own frequency: X/Y = $F01A/$F01B, then on into the start below.
Starts voice 1's vibrato at the frequency in X/Y: current frequency $F01F/$F020 = X/Y, then the counters reload below.
Reloads voice 1's vibrato counters from its setting: step timer $F027 = $F00D, and the step counts of the four phases ($F023-$F026) from $F008-$F00B.
Voice 2's vibrato starts again from the note's own frequency: X/Y = $F045/$F046, then on into the start below.
Starts voice 2's vibrato at the frequency in X/Y: current frequency $F04A/$F04B = X/Y, then the counters reload below.
Reloads voice 2's vibrato counters from its setting: step timer $F052 = $F038, and the step counts of the four phases ($F04E-$F051) from $F033-$F036.
Voice 1, once a frame. If bit 0 of $19 is set, count down its ticks $1A, and at 0 read the next event ($97B4); whatever happens, the effects follow ($9931).
Moves voice 1's place in the tune past a three-byte command, then reads the next event.

Reads the event at voice 1's place. A byte with bit 7 set is a command: its low bits index the handler table $9913, whose word is written into the JMP at $97D5; the two bytes after it go to $16/$17, and the index to $20. Any other byte is a note ($97D8).
Jumps to the command's handler. $97C2 and $97C8 write the operand before every jump, so the address stored here is whichever handler ran last.
Low byte of the JMP at $97D5, written at $97C2 with the low byte of the command's handler.
High byte of the JMP at $97D5, written at $97C8.

A note or a rest. $60 is a rest: it only sets the length ($987F). $5F is taken as note $5F without the transpose; any other note has the transpose $9F46 added (and the carry from the compare, set for $61-$7F) and goes to $18. If voice 1's bit in the enable mask $F081 is clear, the note is silent and only its length is set; otherwise $97F4 starts it.
Never runs: LDA $19 / AND #$08 / BEQ $97EB, a test of voice 1's cut bit that the JMP before it always skips and nothing jumps to.

Starts the note in $18 from voice 1's block at $9EF3. Block bytes $1F-$22 go to the filter, $D415-$D418, with the volume $F082 in place of the mode byte's low four bits. The gate is cleared, then the block's waveform, attack/decay and sustain/release ($1A-$1C) go to $D404-$D406, so the envelope starts again; $F01C keeps the waveform. If the pulse flags (byte $17) are set, the sweep setting (bytes $0F-$19) is copied to $F00F-$F019, and if the vibrato flags (byte $0E) are set, bytes $00-$0E go to $F000-$F00E. The note's frequency from $F0EA (low) and $F08E (high) goes to $D400/$D401 and $F01A/$F01B, and the vibrato starts from it ($974D). The base pulse width (bytes $18/$19) goes to $D402/$D403 and the sweep starts ($970F); the release and gate ticks (bytes $1D/$1E) go to $F01D/$F01E.

$0736 copies the loader's second page here from $C100. In the opening it falls in V1_START_NOTE: the gate is cleared and voice 1's waveform, attack/decay and sustain/release written, then the pulse sweep and vibrato settings copied, the frequency set and the sweep, vibrato and timers started.
The note's length: its second byte indexes the length values at block byte $22 ($9F15) and the value goes to the ticks $1A. Voice 1's place moves on two bytes, then the effects run.
Command $80, return: voice 1's place comes back off its stream stack ($9F26/$9F36, index $1D) and the next event is read.
Command $82: five bytes from the pointer to block bytes $1A-$1E (waveform, attack/decay, sustain/release, release ticks, gate ticks).
Copies Y+1 bytes from the command's pointer into voice 1's block, the last to $9EF3+X, counting both down; then skips the command ($97A9).
Command $86: 35 bytes to block bytes $00-$22, a whole instrument (vibrato, pulse sweep, envelope and filter).
Command $88: 15 bytes to block bytes $00-$0E, the vibrato setting.
Command $8A: 11 bytes to block bytes $0F-$19, the pulse sweep setting.
Command $8C: 16 bytes to block bytes $23-$32, the frames each length index 1-16 lasts.
Command $8E: voice 1 carries on at the pointer.

Command $9C: pushes $97A8 and jumps to the pointer, so the routine there runs as a subroutine and its RTS lands on $97A9, past the command. Voice 1 uses it to fade in ($F400) and out ($F406) and to flip a note ($F495); voice 2's own handler ($9BB7) runs the matching flip at $F553.

Never runs: the transposed call that voices 2 and 3 have (the fourth byte to the transpose $9F46, then the call with 4 as the command's length; the BIT at $98EE hides the LDA #$03). Voice 1's handler table has no entry for it.
Command $90: the place past the command goes on voice 1's stream stack and the voice carries on at the pointer, until a return.

Command $98: the command's third byte goes into voice 1's block at the offset in its second. The tune uses it to change one setting between notes: gate ticks, pulse width, attack/decay, sustain/release, a vibrato delta or flags.

Voice 1's command handlers, one word each for commands $80-$9C, low byte first: return, envelope, stop, instrument, vibrato, pulse, lengths, jump, call, stop, stop, stop, poke, stop, machine code. Stop is MUSIC_STOP ($96A1). $97BF reads the low byte through $9913,X with X = command AND $7F, always even.
The same table one byte on: $97C5 reads the handler's high byte through $9914,X with the same X.

Voice 1's vibrato, every frame while its release counter $F01D is not 0, from the current frequency $F01F/$F020. Nothing changes unless bit 2 of the flags $F00E is set and the frequency is not 0. The delay $F00C counts down first, adding the fourth delta $F006/$F007 each frame when bit 1 is set (a slide away from the written note: VIBRATO_SLIDE takes C#5 up to about D#5). Then the step timer $F027 waits $F00D frames between steps, and each step the first phase with steps left ($F023-$F026) adds its delta ($F000-$F007) and loses a step. When all four are spent, bit 7 starts them again from the note's frequency ($9747), bit 0 from where the pitch is ($9753); with neither the pitch stays.
The frequency to $D400/$D401 and $F01F/$F020.

Voice 1's pulse sweep, from the current width $F021/$F022, when bit 2 of its flags $F017 is set. The delay $F015 counts down, then the step timer $F02A waits $F016 frames between steps; each step adds the first delta ($F00F/$F010) while phase A has steps ($F028), then the second ($F011/$F012) while phase B has ($F029). With both spent, bit 7 starts again from the base width ($9709), bit 0 from the current one ($9715).
The pulse width to $F021/$F022 and $D402/$D403.

Voice 1's note timing: while gate ticks $F01E remain, count them down, and at 0 clear the gate bit ($F01C AND $FE to $D404) so the release begins. After that count the release ticks $F01D down; at 0 clear $D400-$D406 and set bit 3 of $19. With $F01D at 0 the effects stop too ($9931).
A zero byte between voice 1's code and voice 2's; nothing reads it.
Voice 2, once a frame: the same as voice 1 ($979D) with bit 1 of $19, ticks $1B and place $12/$13. Voice 2 has a vibrato and no pulse sweep.
Moves voice 2's place past a three-byte command, then reads the next event.
Reads voice 2's next event: a command goes through the handler table $9BEF into the JMP at $9AC3, with its two bytes in $16/$17; anything else is a note.
Jumps to the command's handler; $9AB0 and $9AB6 write the operand before every jump.
Low byte of voice 2's JMP at $9AC3, written at $9AB0.
High byte of voice 2's JMP at $9AC3, written at $9AB6.
A note or rest on voice 2, as voice 1's ($97D8), with the transpose $9F9A and bit 1 of the enable mask $F081.
Never runs: a test of voice 2's cut bit (bit 4 of $19), skipped by the JMP before it like voice 1's at $97EE.

Starts voice 2's note from its block at $9F47, as voice 1's does: filter from bytes $1F-$22, then gate off and waveform, attack/decay, sustain/release to $D40B-$D40D, $F047 keeping the waveform. The vibrato flags (byte $0E) go to $F039 and, when set, bytes $00-$0E to $F02B-$F039. The frequency goes to $D407/$D408 and $F045/$F046 and the vibrato starts ($9778); the base pulse width goes straight to $D409/$D40A, with no sweep; release and gate ticks to $F048/$F049.
Voice 2's note length from its length values at $9F69 into $1B; the place moves on two bytes.
Command $80 on voice 2: return, off the stream stack $9F7A/$9F8A (index $1E).
Command $82 on voice 2: five bytes to block bytes $1A-$1E.
Copies Y+1 bytes from the pointer into voice 2's block, the last to $9F47+X; then skips the command.
Command $86 on voice 2: 35 bytes to block bytes $00-$22.
Command $92 on voice 2: 51 bytes to block bytes $00-$32, an instrument and the 16 length values together.
Command $88 on voice 2: 15 bytes to block bytes $00-$0E.
Command $8A on voice 2: 11 bytes to block bytes $0F-$19. The tune never uses it, and voice 2 has no sweep to use them.
Command $9A on voice 2: the fourth byte becomes the transpose $9F9A, then the jump below.
Command $8E on voice 2: carry on at the pointer.
Command $9C on voice 2: pushes $9A98 and jumps to the pointer; the routine's RTS lands on $9A99, past the command.
Command $90 on voice 2: push the place past the command (A = 3, or 4 from $9BE4) on the stream stack and carry on at the pointer.
Command $98 on voice 2: the third byte into voice 2's block at the offset in the second.

Command $96 on voice 2: the fourth byte becomes the transpose $9F9A, then the call with 4 as the command's length. Voice 2 plays its broken chords this way, four eight-note patterns ($F562, $F579, $F58D, $F59E) each at many pitches, and the four-note $F692 of its closing chords.

Voice 2's command handlers for $80-$9C, low byte first: return, envelope, stop, instrument, vibrato, pulse, stop, jump, call, instrument and lengths, stop, transposed call, poke, transposed jump, machine code. $9AAD reads the low bytes through $9BEF,X.
Voice 2's handler table one byte on, for the high bytes ($9AB3).
Voice 2's vibrato, the same as voice 1's ($9931) on its own state: setting $F02B-$F039, counters $F04E-$F052, current frequency $F04A/$F04B, written to $D407/$D408.
The frequency to $D407/$D408 and $F04A/$F04B.
Voice 2's note timing, as voice 1's ($9A64): gate ticks $F049, then release ticks $F048; at the end $D407-$D40D are cleared and bit 4 of $19 set.
Voice 3, once a frame: as voice 1, with bit 2 of $19, ticks $1C and place $14/$15. Voice 3 has a pulse sweep and no vibrato.
Moves voice 3's place past a three-byte command, then reads the next event.

ZERO_PAGE_BACKUP ($A000-$A0FF) - the KERNAL's zero page, kept here while the game works in
the real one. OPENING_SETUP copies it here ($06B2); SWAP_ZERO_PAGE_AND_BACKUP ($053C)
exchanges the two around a part's load (PREPARE_DISK_IO $04FB, END_DISK_IO $0521), so the
KERNAL's LOAD runs with its own zero page while the game's waits here. The game calls SCNKEY
and GETIN with no swap. Rather than saving individual locations, $053C exchanges the two
images, $02-$FF, wholesale: for each
index it loads the live byte, loads the backup byte, writes the backup value live, and writes
the live value into the backup. One routine therefore serves both directions - calling it
twice restores the original state - and there is no separate "restore" entry point.
053C  LDY #$FF
053E  LDA $0000,Y     ; live zero-page byte
0541  TAX
0542  LDA $A000,Y     ; corresponding backup byte
0545  STA $0000,Y     ; backup -> live
0548  TXA
0549  STA $A000,Y     ; live -> backup
054C  DEY
054D  CPY #$01        ; stop before index $01
054F  BNE $053E
C64 SPECIFIC, AND THE REASON FOR THE ODD LOOP BOUND: the loop runs Y = $FF down to $02 and
deliberately never touches $0000 and $0001. On a 6510 those two addresses are not RAM but the
CPU's on-chip I/O port - $0001 is the bank-select register that decides whether BASIC, KERNAL,
I/O or RAM is visible at $A000-$BFFF and $D000-$FFFF, and $0000 is its data-direction
register. Swapping a stale value into $0001 would change the memory map underneath the
running code, for instance banking BASIC ROM over the backup at $A000 that the loop is reading;
the routine itself, at $053C, is in RAM that no value of $01 hides. Banking is managed
separately, by explicit stores to $01.
Note the backup lives at $A000-$BFFF RAM, i.e. underneath the BASIC ROM image, which is
exactly the region the $01 value chosen by this game leaves as RAM.
At the opening, $A002-$A0FF holds zero page as OPENING_SETUP copied it there ($06B2), before the tune took over $10-$21.

PAYLOAD FORMAT - identical to a RoomGraphicRecord payload with width = 4 cells and
height = 4 character rows. The source stream is interleaved per character row:
32 bytes  bitmap      (4 cells x 8 scanlines)
4 bytes  screen matrix
4 bytes  colour RAM
------------------------------------------------
40 bytes per character row, 4 rows = 160 bytes per icon
BLIT_ROOM_GRAPHIC ($05BF) / COPY_BLIT_ROW ($0676) scatter those three spans to three different
destinations, which is why they are interleaved rather than stored as three flat planes.
C64 DISPLAY SEMANTICS (for a reader fluent in 6510 but not in VIC-II)
The picture band runs in multicolor bitmap mode: RASTER_SPLIT_PICTURE ($A7E3) sets $D011=$3B
(BMM=1, bitmap mode), $D016=$D8 (MCM=1, multicolor), $D018=$38 (video matrix $CC00, bitmap
$E000, both inside VIC bank 3) and $D021=$00. In that mode the VIC consumes TWO bitmap bits per
pixel, so horizontal resolution halves - each 8x8 cell is 4 double-wide pixels across - and the
colour of a pixel is selected by the bit pair:
00 -> background register $D021
01 -> high nybble of that cell's screen-matrix byte
10 -> low  nybble of that cell's screen-matrix byte
11 -> low  nybble of that cell's colour-RAM byte
Hence the 4 screen bytes and 4 colour bytes per row: they carry three of the four palette
entries for the four cells in that row. An icon is 32 x 32 screen pixels (16 double-wide
multicolor pixels wide).

RASTER_IRQ_DISPATCH ($A7E0)
Purpose: The gameplay interrupt handler, installed in the KERNAL RAM vector CINV. A CLC followed by a BCC whose offset byte at $A7E2 is self-modified selects one of the three raster-split phase bodies, so successive interrupts cycle picture, text and bottom.
Inputs: The offset byte at $A7E2 holds $00, $27 or $52, selecting $A7E3, $A80A or $A835 respectively. The processor has pushed the return address and status register, and the KERNAL's hardware IRQ entry at $FF48 has pushed A, X and Y.
Outputs: The selected phase reprograms the VIC, arms the next raster compare, rewrites the offset byte for the following interrupt, acknowledges the VIC interrupt latch and chains to the KERNAL epilogue at $EA81, which pulls the registers and executes RTI.
Assumptions: Requires $01=$06: $A000-$BFFF must read as RAM, and the KERNAL ROM must be in view for the hardware vector at $FFFE (to $FF48) and the exit at $EA81 (with $05 the CPU would take the vector from RAM, which holds $77AC, so the game writes $05 only with interrupts masked); banking BASIC back in while this vector is live would vector the interrupt into ROM. It relies entirely on the KERNAL prologue for register preservation, so it must never be entered by a foreground JSR.
Clobbers: A and flags within the handler; the interrupted A, X, Y, status, stack context and program counter are all restored by the KERNAL epilogue. The offset byte at $A7E2 is rewritten every interrupt.
Hardware changes: Through the selected phase: VIC-II $D011, $D016, $D018, $D021, $D012 and $D019. CINV itself is not modified here.

RESTORE_SYSTEM_TO_BASIC ($A893)
Purpose: Hand the machine back to the KERNAL in a state a stock C64 can survive: select a memory map with the KERNAL ROM in view (BASIC's ROM at $A000-$BFFF stays banked out), zero the low RAM pages, rebuild the KERNAL indirect vector block, re-run BASIC's vector and zero-page initialisation, and restore the stock IRQ handler.
Inputs: None. Physically located inside a dead object-icon slot, which is why it survives in the icon table region.
Outputs: $01 = $06; $0002-$0101, $0200-$02FF and $0300-$03FF zeroed (the STA $0002,Y loop runs Y=$00..$FF, so it spills two bytes into the stack page); $B2/$B3 = $033C (the cassette-buffer pointer) and $C2 = 3; the 32-byte KERNAL default vector table copied from $FD30 to $0314-$0333; BASIC's indirect vectors and zero page reinitialised through KERNAL $E453 and $E3BF; CINV ($0314/$0315) = $EA31.
Assumptions: $01 must be set first, because everything afterwards reads KERNAL ROM. Note the consequence for its own neighbourhood: with $06 selected, $A000-$BFFF still reads as RAM, so this code and the icon table around it remain reachable, while $E000-$FFFF is ROM, which is why the game's own character set at $F800 becomes invisible to the CPU though the VIC-II still sees it. Nothing in the engine or the three parts calls it.
Clobbers: A, X, Y, flags, zero page from $02 (and $0100-$0101), pages 2 and 3, and BASIC's workspace. X is destroyed by the KERNAL calls to $E453 and $E3BF.
Hardware changes: Writes the 6510 port $01. Rewrites the KERNAL RAM vector block $0314-$0333 including CINV. Calls KERNAL $E453 and $E3BF. Does not itself touch VIC-II, SID or CIA registers, but restoring CINV to $EA31 hands interrupt-driven keyboard scanning and jiffy timing back to the KERNAL.

INSTALL_GAME_IRQ ($A8CC)
Purpose: Point the KERNAL RAM interrupt vector at the game's raster-split dispatcher, clear CIA 1's FLAG interrupt mask and discard any pending CIA 1 request. It undoes the last step of RESTORE_SYSTEM_TO_BASIC, which points CINV back at $EA31 and leaves $DC0D alone.
Inputs: None. Also located inside a dead object-icon slot.
Outputs: CINV ($0314/$0315) = $A7E0; CIA 1's FLAG interrupt mask cleared; any latched CIA 1 interrupt request discarded.
Assumptions: Requires $01=$06 so that $A7E0 is the game's handler in RAM rather than BASIC ROM, and requires the raster source and initial compare to have been configured already. Nothing in the engine or the three parts calls it; $070F installs $A7E0 itself, at $076D.
Clobbers: A and flags.
Hardware changes: Writes the KERNAL RAM IRQ vector at $0314/$0315. Writes $10 to CIA 1 interrupt control $DC0D: with bit 7 clear the one bits are cleared, so this clears the FLAG mask and leaves the other sources alone. Then reads $DC0D, whose read side reports and clears the pending latch and releases the IRQ line, guaranteeing no stale CIA request fires when interrupts are re-enabled.
